attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post, written in his voice.

semantics.note: The draft keeps the 'nearly a hundred billion dollars each' threshold. 'Not making much from AI' is a fair paraphrase of 'aren't rolling in cash' in this AI-revenue context. 'For no real reason' is a value judgment and can't be tested.

contract.note: Reading the amount as each company's 2025 annual capex budget is the ordinary reading, given the capex discussion around it. Treating total capex as an upper bound on data-center spending is reasonable and stated openly. The profit and 'no real reason' parts are left out of scoring.

evidence.note: Meta's Q1 2025 10-Q (via a mirror), filed before publication, puts its whole 2025 capex budget at $64–72B. Data-center spending can't exceed that, which is well short of nearly $100B.
Alphabet's CFO said on April 24, 2025 that total 2025 capex would be about $75B. Total capex is a valid upper bound, so it also falls materially short. This is a company disclosure.

reviews.rationale: The claim says each company is spending nearly $100B. Budgets disclosed before July 21, 2025 put Meta's whole capex at no more than $72B and Alphabet's at about $75B. Both are upper bounds on data-center spending and well below nearly $100B, so the 'each' claim is contradicted. The profit wording and 'for no real reason' are not settled by this evidence.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: Revision 2 restored the infrastructure clause, so the proposition now matches the statement. It is a present-tense judgment about OpenAI's financial position at the time.

contract.note: Reading it as a claim about OpenAI's financial position at publication, not a forecast that it can never be profitable, is fair. Whether a path is 'workable' has no stated test, so the result depends on interpretation.

evidence.note: A Reuters report of Bloomberg's account of OpenAI's own projections: positive cash flow by 2029 and revenue over $125B. This shows a proposed path, not that the path is workable, and it doesn't rule one out either.
OpenAI's own announcement of $40B in new funding, partly to scale compute. It confirms reliance on outside capital at that point, but not that the reliance must continue.

reviews.rationale: The packet has OpenAI's projected path to cash-flow positivity and evidence that it depended on outside funding at the time. Neither shows the path was workable or rules it out, and the packet has no complete financial model. The contract's support and contradiction conditions are both unmet.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words, presented as established fact in his post.

semantics.note: The universal claim and the Midjourney exception are both kept. The sentence states firm facts, even though the section heading uses 'likely'.

contract.note: The population follows Zitron's own scope: companies that build models or build on others' models. Company-wide profit is the plain reading. The quarter is the evaluator's choice and the accounting basis is unspecified.

evidence.note: Gamma's CEO said in a July 3, 2025 interview that the company had 'been profitable'. This challenges the universal claim, but it is the company's own unaudited statement with no period or accounting basis given.

reviews.rationale: Disproving the universal claim needs one comparable profitable company. The only candidate is Gamma, and the only evidence is its CEO's own statement, with no defined period or profit measure. The packet also can't show losses across the whole population. Neither condition is met.

attribution.note: Zitron's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The draft captures the claim that Agentforce is a chatbot platform that isn't autonomous or agentic. It slightly drops his concession that the bots can plug into APIs, but the contract keeps it.

contract.note: Zitron said 'by any reasonable definition', so testing against an ordinary industry definition of an agent is fair. That definition is software that picks and runs configured actions without a human directing each step. Not requiring job replacement is fair under his own wording.

evidence.note: Salesforce developer guide, April 2025. It documents triggering agents from Flow, Apex and REST, outside chat, and agent-to-agent orchestration. This is technical documentation by the company itself.

Salesforce developer guide, January 2025. It says the reasoning engine chooses and orchestrates configured actions, such as updating an order's status. This is architectural background from before the target quarter.
The CRMArena-Pro benchmark measures how reliable LLM agents are at tasks. It says nothing about whether Agentforce can take actions.

reviews.rationale: Dated Salesforce technical documentation shows Agentforce agents could be triggered programmatically outside chat and could orchestrate configured actions beyond retrieving information. That meets the contract's contradiction condition for the claim that it was only a chatbot and no agent by any reasonable definition. Low reliability scores bear on performance, not on whether it is an agent.
